And then from there, I walked slowly and on foot, having covered 2 or 3 kilometres, I -- after that, there was -- another military vehicle came along and I hitched a ride and I managed to return to the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're not sure on which date this took place?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they saying that these people were going to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything of the kind, any such stories. This -- when this gentleman came out, he was probably an officer but he didn't have any insignia, so I don't know. I didn't ask, of course. And he just told us, You try and get yourselves rides to your -- and he also said, If you remain here, if you stay on here, I'll tell people to find you a ride in a vehicle going to Drinjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that escorting the convoy was a vehicle that you identified as a Pitzgauer?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a UN-marked vehicle, a white vehicle, at the end or at the front of the column?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot say that I saw one when I didn't see one. As I told the investigators in Banja Luka, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us at approximately what time was it when you were in front of the Zvornik Brigade, what time of the day was it?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, because I do not want the same thing to happen when I mentioned some things before here. And I believe it was in the afternoon, but I cannot say exactly. Because I know when later I came -- I arrived in the Bratunac Brigade and I was on duty at -- that night, I believe I stated it was between the 13th and the 14th, but I cannot claim that with certainty. That was the first time I saw Mr. Blagojevic leaving the command, as he went out of the command. That was, in fact, the first time I saw him in that command at all. And after a couple of days, after all this, I struck up a conversation with someone. And I said to someone, Well, Mr. Blagojevic is here. And then that person said, Well, he is the commander. And I really didn't know until the Srebrenica thing had passed that he had been appointed commander of the Bratunac Brigade and all that. And I said yesterday -- you have all these facts and data. And I think that he was the 10th or 15th commander of that brigade. This is something that I wasn't at all interested in who was on what position. I was just an ordinary soldier. I was only carrying out my orders. What else can I say? Nothing. There is nothing more that I can say. I've tried to say several times here that really when I made certain statements, I may have made a mistake in certain respects. I'm not avoiding any responsibility. If I am accountable for anything, for war crimes, for perjury, or for giving false testimony, I'm not seeking to evade responsibility, if need be, right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you provided your previous statement, you had the status of suspect, and this is what your -- this was well-known to you?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that is the same at this moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you were told that you did not know how long this status of yours would last?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't speak with the Prosecutor, the gentlemen for the Prosecution at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you gave your statement in light of a family problem that you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that also disturb you while you were giving the statement?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what this is all about, tell them freely. You are protected here and you should be protected here while you are giving your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, I think this issue is not quite relevant to the subject matter of this case, and it will give tremendous suffering to this witness. So would you please withdraw this question and try to wrap up your cross-examination as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will be bringing it to a close. I just have one more topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We really do not wish to place you in any uncomfortable position with your testimony here, Radenko. Just one more thing I want to clarify. You were speaking about this on topic a little bit earlier. Can we go on?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This man who came out who you described as a tall man with a white belt, a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify one sentence that you mentioned here, and that this was, as you said, a tall man. And you indicated to the investigator who was present, Bruce Bursik?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, could you please tell us what type of a person was this, what are the characteristics, the physical characteristics of Bruce Bursik?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give his precise height but it could be between 180 to 190 centimetres, 1.8, 1.9 metres, and about 40 or so years old, perhaps a little younger or a little older by a few years. I cannot say that precisely. I cannot give you a precise estimate about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was wearing white belts?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know who this person is?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I just wanted to finish with one more question. You said that this military police officer at the gate said that the rest of the buses should not enter?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. One bus went in, and the second started to go in, but then he stopped it and it stopped. This -- as you could see yourself, if you were down there you know that there is room to stop there. So that is where we got out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you to the witness. I apologise if there was anything which could bring you into an uncomfortable position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, there is just one issue to clarify. Re-examined by Mr. Waespi:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have been asked by Mr. Karnavas about the 13th of July, and you indicated you went to the compound where UNPROFOR was. And then you said, and I quote you: "They allowed us to come in with the buses." Now, can you tell us first, who is "they"? Who allowed you to come in?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he was an officer or he was just standing there at the entrance, at the ramp. They had their soldiers there at the ramp at the entrance to the base. This was a battery factory. We had to leave our weapons at the entrance, leave them with them. And to go down there to board the people on the buses. We were not to go into the base with weapons, but we were to accompany the buses into the base. On our way out of the base, we would take our weapons. And now I cannot tell you whether he was a corporal or a captain or I don't know what his rank was. I think at the time there were Dutch soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. And you talk about "we," that you were allowed to get in. Were there other members of the military police with you at the time who was allowed in?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about four or five of us there perhaps, who just happened to be there. Somebody said we should go and accompany the buses, somebody who was down there, to go to this base, to the UNPROFOR base, whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Like you, members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall -- you just told us that somebody said we should go. Can you tell us who the somebody was.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, because there were a lot of commanders there from the corps, from the Drina Corps. Because this was -- well, General Krstic was there and I don't know who else. I don't really -- he was there the most -- well, as the commander of the Drina Corps. At the time, he was thought to be the commander of the Drina Corps. So just like they say that Mr. Blagojevic was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. And he was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm sure you would recall if it was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It calls for speculation. The witness answered. Now we're trying to get the witness to -- a multiple choice in hopes of making some sort of record for an argument down the road. He asked a question; he should live with the answer. The gentleman indicated he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe Mr. Waespi has not finished his question. I think you are speculating at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm a little bit clairvoyant on this one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's hear what the question is put by Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get an order from General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. Whether he told somebody else or, as they say, somebody conveyed that. But from him directly, I did not get any orders. Whether he gave to some of the people who were there, some of his men, because those people who were around him, I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it wasn't him you got the order from to go into the compound?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A man came to us. He was dark. He combed his hair upwards and he said, A couple of you that are standing there should go. There were about four or five of us. I don't know exactly how many of us there were. Some were there near the factory. He said, Take this bus and go to the bus so that people can get on and the women and children who were down there so that they can be transported towards the end point and so on, to their destination. I don't know what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. At this stage are there any documents to tender. Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what the procedures are for 92 bis statements, but that would be the right moment to tender it. And I think the exhibit number would be P685.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This document, 685, is admitted into the evidence. Are there any documents on the part of the Defence that would like to be tendered. Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We do not, Your Honour, have any documents to tender, although I would, again, ask that at some point the translators would look at page 40, line 5 to 7, and if they could -- it wasn't -- the question was never re-asked and just for the sake of having a clear record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. I believe that the translators after our sitting will check the transcript. And I hope they could, through the Registrar, give you an answer to that. Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would like to use this opportunity to tender D62. This is a document that you have in front of you, but I would just like it to be admitted with the markings that the witness made today on this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. This document, D62/3, is admitted into the evidence. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home. Thank you. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, now I think it's time to deal with your housekeeping matters. As you probably understand that at the meeting a document this Trial Chamber would like to reiterate the three criteria we mentioned in the guidelines. One is the reliability, the other is the relevancy, the third one is the probative value of that. I hope your submission could concentrate on these three points.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe that it has probative value and it was already accepted as evidence in the Krstic trial, so it must have been proven reliable. We have no objections from the Prosecution. It's offered, not to prove the contents of the document being offered, but to show that the circumstances involved -- it's the only raw material, only recording, that we have that exists in the Tribunal, as far as I know, from the Okresanica [Realtime transcript read in error "Orahovac"] facility. And we're using this document to show the circumstances and the recording abilities and the process that they must deal with at Okresanica [Realtime transcript read in error "Orahovac"] with five of these going on at one time. This witness, of course, could not testify to Okresanica [Realtime transcript read in error "Orahovac"], but he did testify that this is a normal recording and he recognised it as something that he was accustomed to listening to. I think as an offer of proof for the lack of authenticated process, the lack of reliability of intercepts, this should be offered into evidence to show the process that all of the communications centres had to go through. And it is the only evidence -- the best evidence that we have to offer at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that you do not want the contents to be translated into a language that we understand; you just want to show the circumstances. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you tell us so far as you know what is the date of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I believe it's the first week in August, but they couldn't verify that because it's a continuing tape. It's the first week of August from the Okresanica facility. It is not July 14th, 1995, which would have been, as the witness testified, a much heavier traffic day. So this just shows a normal day, August 1995, versus July 14th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see Mr. Stojanovic is standing. Do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like -- I think on page 56 two times on line 14 and line 10 it was stated instead of Okresanica, it was said Orahovac. Just for the transcript, this is just a slip. So this is a recording that originates from Okresanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have the interpreters check it out after the sitting. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And I thank my learned colleague for pointing that out. But we would like to offer, even though untimely, D61/3, into evidence for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. McCloskey, are you sure that this is the tape-recording in your possession or in the whole Tribunal, as Ms. Sinatra claimed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure which tape this is. There is a tape that is, I believe, a tape like Ms. Sinatra says that we think is a tape from August from Okresanica that we think reflects the recordings as they occurred. We also have a tape that we think are a collection of intercepts that the intel people had, which is different, obviously, from something that is recorded live. I think Ms. Sinatra is probably correct that it's the first one she's talking about. She's -- we provided that material with her and she had an expert. So I don't have a reason to doubt that. There are other tapes for other time periods. But for the period that was anywhere near relevant, it really comes down to these two tapes that I have described, and that's really August. I think one of the, one of the tapes that we think is a collection had a 13 July conversation in it, but it didn't really have much relevance to anything that anyone has commented on. So that's in answer to your question about tapes. In particular regarding their -- I would object to this piece of evidence coming in under this particular witness. As I recall his testimony, he said that from his position in Dekic, they listened to only one person at a time speaking on the frequency. He said that -- my recollection is that the tape that we played for him was not the same as the kind of material he listened so. Because as we all heard, you could hear a couple of people speaking in the background and it was -- it's different. He believe, I said, that's the kind like the other guys would get on the mountaintop. So while I think it was interesting to hear it and hear his comments on it and it did provide us some idea about what he listened to, in that regard it may be helpful for the Court. I don't see how it's now helpful to have that in evidence, especially since we don't know what is said in it. And this really isn't the witness for this tape. If counsel has an expert and is challenging the Okresanica material, then perhaps at a later date it would be relevant. But for what this witness said about it, all that is really relevant is that he said not the kind of material that he was listening to. So he's really not the right witness. But for whatever value you think it may be, that would be the Prosecution's submission. I don't -- I think it came into the record. We heard it. What else do we need it for, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are not debating here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I would just like to respond to his submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, sir. What I see is that of course Mr. Jokic is innocent until proven guilty, so there may not ever be an opportunity to present a Defence expert witness in this trial, which I would hope would be the case. Second of all, the Trial Chamber has rightly said that now the Defence, once they filed their objections to intercepts, after the final witness would be allowed to supplement this -- these objections to intercepts with another written submission. I would ask the Court maybe to reserve their decision on the admission of this evidence until you read the further submissions of the Defence regarding the further evidence that we have received since we've filed our objections to the intercept. And I believe that the Trial Chamber has given us orally an opportunity to respond to this last witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could be -- could briefly be heard also on this issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to open Pandora's box.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're not, Your Honour. But what -- it affects, it affects me, too. Rulings do in fact do affect us as well. Directly commenting on Mr. McCloskey's remarks. First and foremost, I think the tape may be relevant because it may go to the weight. I know that issue is still open, whether the -- all these notebooks come in. But it does assist in giving -- to the issue of weight. Now, Mr. McCloskey is quite correct that perhaps this was not the best witness to get this piece of evidence in; however, be that as it may the issue was still pending and therefor is still ripe and the request being made by Ms. Sinatra is not at all untimely in my opinion. Also, we did have the benefit from this particular expert, if we could call him that, in intercepts to say that there was a distinction. And I think his comments in relation to that particular tape are also very helpful. I think the -- I agree with Mr. McCloskey, it's already in evidence in the sense that we heard about it. However, since the issue is under consideration and it goes to the weight and at some point it may be necessary for the Court to re-listen to the tape, I think that the request is not only reasonable but it's also timely. And I think it does have some probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after my discussions with my colleagues and hearing the submissions by the parties, we believe that Ms. Sinatra has established the relevance and the probative value to this piece of the documents. Of course we understand that the Defence did not ask for the translation of the contents of this piece of the evidence into the language that we understand. She just wanted to show a kind of comparison and the quality of the tapes. So in this way, this Trial Chamber decided to have it admitted into the evidence as a document D61/3, only for the purpose of comparison of the quality of the tapes. It is so decided. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Just to clarify. Is that exhibit just the three-minute section or was it the whole tape so we know what we're getting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have recorded for the Registry here just the one minute and 50 seconds that we played in the courtroom. So it's very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's a very brief part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get just a copy of that so we know what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course. I think it's a reasonable request.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I might clarify. It's their Prosecution exhibit that they allowed us to listen to. The first one minute and 50 seconds, tape 1, side A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record, it is not our exhibit. It was something we provided, but just to -- so we are all clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'll provide a copy for the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sure. That's the right word. Well, I think we'll have the break and we'll resume at 5 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, good evening, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good evening, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please stand up and make the solemn declaration, please. I did not get any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Viada.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Good evening, Your Honours. Good evening, Defence counsel. This is a witness that asked for some protective measures particularly pseudonym and face distortion. Examined by Mr. Viada:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could have a look at this paper and tell us if your name is written on it, but not tell your name out loud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you currently serving in the Royal Dutch Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your rank when you were in the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: 1st lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve in the Srebrenica enclave with the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you arrive in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: In January 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to the days before the fall of Srebrenica, what were -- who were your duties in the previous days to the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: I was part of the Recce Platoon which was attached to the Dutch Battalion in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: In Potocari at the main compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day before the fall of Srebrenica, what were your jobs at that moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: I was on an observation near Srebrenica just on the east side, and observing to the south the movements of the Bosnian Serb troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until which day did you remain at that place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: That was until the day before the enclave fell, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you leave the observation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Because I wasn't able to do my job there, and the pressure was very high. And we got held back to the compound.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that the pressure was very high, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: That the Bosnian Serb army was already entering Srebrenica from the south, and we were not able to monitor anything from the east. So we were at a very vulnerable location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: We went back to the main compound, Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue in Potocari that day -- sorry. I have to go back. At what time did you go back to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: That was the night before the actual falling of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: I -- it was at night. I can't remember. It was late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Late.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Like after 11.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that night did you sleep or did you continue on duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: We left the observation post, and we also left some people behind. We were negotiating first to get them from that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived to Potocari, did you continue doing the same job that you were doing before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes, up until a certain point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why? Could you be more precise with this. Why did you stop doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: The next day we got told to stop controlling aircraft on targets, otherwise the people, the Dutch army people who were taken from the observation post around the enclave, especially from the south, they said they are going to kill them one by one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: That came via -- from the commander of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who were those soldiers that were sentenced with death?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Those were the soldiers that were taken from the OPs, who were captured the week before in the south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in your -- in the proofing, proofing session, one name of the person who conveyed that message to the Dutch Battalion. Do you remember that name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I got it -- I say I didn't get it from the commander directly, it was Colonel Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who is that Colonel Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No, I couldn't make a face with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then after you were ordered to stop doing this job that you were doing before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: After that, the -- actually we kept the aircraft at a safe distance. And it went real quick after that that the enclave really fell. And we were taking refugees on the compound and we were, you know, trying to get hold of the situation. It was a big chaos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges at what time approximately did the refugees start to arrive to the United Nations compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: They arrived pretty early in the surrounding, but they wouldn't let up -- on the compound. And it started with the wounded. And after that, I can't remember exactly times it started happening. And they were making -- they were actually splitting in urgency who was getting in the compound and who was put in the buildings, the industrial buildings, close to the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many refugees would you estimate were present in and around the compound at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Then I have to make a real estimation. It might be 15.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your estimation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: That's an estimation, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate, what is the percentage of those refugees -- what percentage of those refugees were women and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: I cannot estimate that, no. But I know that most men left in the hills to the west of Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so, what is your estimation? Were there more women or more men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: I can't remember if it was really actually more men and women. That's ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any commitment with regards to the civilians at that moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Can you explain that question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have some kind of orders regarding the situation with the civilians at that particular moment just after the refugees were arriving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes. We did not really interfere with them. We -- they were held in the compound, but we were in a separate part of the compound with our unit. So we didn't really interfere with the refugees at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were there refugees out the compound, the compound limit, I mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Outside the compound limit?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Because there were too many refugees according to the surface of the compound area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no room then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Next was that the enclave actually fell. The first soldiers from the Bosnian Serb army entered the enclave, and we saw them walking to the enclave relaxed. I think the decision was already made at that point. And the next time I remember there was a delegation led into the compound to look for war criminals under the Bosnian refugees on the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you accompany that delegation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: After that, we got orders -- or we heard that there was an agreement made to transport all refugees out of the compound to the west. We didn't know where exactly at that time. And we were ordered to escort them by car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these people going to be transported?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: They were transported by, I think, every vehicle that was available in the area, so buses, trucks, everything you can imagine that holds more than --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many buses, approximate, were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: I can't answer that question, because there were buses coming in and going out and coming back. But the whole road in front of the compound was filled with trucks, buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the buses enter the compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No. They stayed on the road outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the Muslim people getting on those buses and trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes. At first they were very scared, of course, to get out of the compound, and after that they were entering -- or actually, leading or being led to the buses to get taken out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was leading the people to go on to the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: There were several people doing that and -- actually, the elderly and the women, they were led on the buses directly. And the men were taken to the white house just across the road of the entrance of the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there some kind of commander or something like that who was in command of these people, soldiers I mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: At that moment I cannot remember, at that moment. It was starting up the whole process and it was very hard. It was a big chaos. There was a lot of panic among the people. And we from DutchBat didn't know what was happening at the time also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that women and the elderly were allowed to go on to the buses and the men were separated and led to another place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you, with the help of the usher, an exhibit that has been admitted into evidence and is Prosecution 2.6. Do you recognise the house depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the house you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: That's the house across the entrance of the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might just -- it's almost comical. There's a big sign that says "white house" on the photo. A blind person can see that label on top of the house. It is so suggestive. I don't know what to make of it at this point, but frankly, I don't think that this identification means anything. We're not disputing that there was a white house, we're not disputing that men were taken to the white house. But I do think if we're going to be showing witnesses these sorts of documents, we don't put a big label on it, "white house," in yellow actually, so it sticks out and say, Is this the house? That's my comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you for your comment. Do you have another photo without any labels or from different angles?

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: I'm afraid I have no other photo right now, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Maybe you could find another one overnight and show this to this witness tomorrow. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these men being treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: They were just led to the -- to that white house across the street, and DutchBat also agreed that people from our unit were allowed to go in there to monitor that which happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see -- did you recall some kind of -- something wrong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: At the beginning, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Later on I have seen one guy got beaten up in the bus pretty bad, and that's the only thing I have seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the men who were in the houses left -- I mean in the house, left at any point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: It was very hard to predict, but there were also buses in front of the white house and they were loaded with men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any commitment with those refugees during the evacuation agreed before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: As I said, we were ordered to transport the convoys of the buses out -- to take the refugees out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: The same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how was the escort of the buses organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Also a little bit chaotic. It was very hard to tell how many would you says were in the convoy and left without telling us. So we really had to look real good and follow the buses that were going out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what were the masses that were taken by your commanders in order to organise this evacuation, this escort, of the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: They put us on a stand-by next to the road and as soon as buses left, we followed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your instructions regarding the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Just to follow the buses and, as I told, there were so many buses. We didn't have enough cars to provide enough security for the convoy. We were able to only escort with one car. So it was more a -- to give a good feeling for the refugees that there would be UN soldiers with the convoy when they were led out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as I understand there was only one car for one convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: It ended up with only one car per one convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally escort any of these convoys, the first convoy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who ordered you to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: That was -- we were ordered by the -- via the battalion commander, by my boss.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many vehicles, approximately, did the convoy that you escorted consist of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was about eight buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Eight buses. And where was your car escorting --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yeah, we were driving right behind the convoy, behind the last bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you -- I would like to show you another exhibit, admitted into evidence already, it is P20.1. It is a map. Could you show the Judges on the map the route that you took out of Potocari that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: We drove from Potocari to Bratunac, and there we took a left to the west and drove north of the enclave. And then up to the south to Milici, Vlasenica, up till as far as I remember it was the Luke area. And what we saw or what we heard is that the refugees were led out of the buses and they had to walk 10 to 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it take to travel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: I can't remember it exactly, but it took a lot longer than we thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see if there were men among the people you were escorting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes, but only elderly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. After the people were allowed to go, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yeah, we didn't know what was the next thing to happen, so we drove back on the road to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time approximately did you return to the compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Again, that is hard to remember. It was in July and it was already dark when we arrived, so it must be around midnight. It was late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: The convoys were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, I mean that night --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes, the convoys were not driving that night, so we were not escorting them also. So we had to wait for the next morning to continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you have to do the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: The next day we had the same task, to escort the convoys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have vehicles, because you said before that you had not enough vehicles to escort the -- otherwise the situation was better or worse at the moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: It was about the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: The overall situation was a little bit better because we knew what was going on at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you just escort another convoy this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: That was the next day, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the next day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: It was the day after when I arrived back at midnight at the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us what happened with the next escort that you helped with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes. We were also stand-by on the road of the compound. We were waiting, and actually it was -- there were buses loading with men -- or elderly men and women. But at the same time two buses with men were leaving from the parking area in front of the white house. So I called my boss to ask him to follow which bus, which group of buses. And they ordered me to follow the two buses with the men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the process of filling these two buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes. It happened in front of us, but there was no significant things going on at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you served [sic] some kind of an incident with a man who was beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes, it was all at the end --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not at the moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the Muslim men on the buses treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: They were all real quite and they looked scared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They looked scared. Did they have any reason to be scared?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, that calls for speculation on the part of the witness. He can observe what they're doing but now he's asking for a speculation on the part of, Did they have any reason to be scared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to say it another way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see personally any violence or mistreatment against any of those men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your orders regarding these buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: To follow those buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many members of the Dutch Battalion were with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And only one United Nations vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes, only one UN vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Bosnian Serb soldiers in the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes. There were -- with every bus, there was at least one at each door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With what action were these buses travelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Initially they were going the same way, and up until the intersection in Bratunac they were going straight instead to go -- they didn't go left to the west as the other convoy did the night before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I show you, with the help of Mr. Usher, an exhibit that has been marked with P677. Can you take the pointer and point to the Judges the normal route that the buses leaving Potocari should have taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm going to re-urge Mr. Karnavas's objection that there can be no independent identification of the area he's talking about when everything is already marked and explained to him. If he's going to identify anything on the map, it shouldn't be labelled -- pre-labelled by the Prosecution as to the areas that he is supposed to identify. And if he is -- if he's marked this document at another time, it would be better as evidence in this Trial Chamber that he independently marked it here in front of the Trial Chamber instead of -- who knows what the circumstances were during the proofing session. A clean copy of this map without labels and for this -- identification purposes for these witnesses would be preferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But I believe that we used this map before many, many times and witnesses marked such maps during the proofing session. There's no objections from the Defence part, so we let this practice go. And now we don't know the purpose for the Prosecution to use this map. So we'll see where the Prosecution is going to lead us. You may proceed, Mr. Viada.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking again, could you take the pointer and point the normal route that the bus leaving Potocari should have taken.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: The normal route was out from Potocari, they were driving to the north, and took the intersection to the west, to the road north of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which was the direction that this bus -- these buses with men took?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Initially he put on his blinker at one of the intersections to take the normal route. And -- but he continued straight. And I cannot remember the exact route he took, because we took kind of a detour through Bratunac. It looked like they -- at that time they discovered that they were being followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other day in our office you put a mark on this exhibit. You can see this circle. What does -- what is the meaning of that circle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Both buses stopped at this location in a corner in front of the big, big building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a building was it where the buses stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: It was a school building -- it looked like a school building. It wasn't confirmed by me, because as far as I remember there were no signs on it. But it had big windows with glass inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: There were soldiers on the street in that vicinity, and then the buses stopped. The men were -- they stayed in the buses. And one soldier who was at that location at that time came up to our vehicle and told us that it was better to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it friendly conversation or was it some kind of argument?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No, not at all. It was a very friendly conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it only one -- did you say soldier or man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: That was a -- I can't remember his rank, but he was in military clothes and had an AK47.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only one soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: There was only one soldier approaching our vehicles, but there were more in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: I did ask him why he wanted us to leave, and he said, It's just better to leave. Then I called my boss at that location. We still had coms with the headquarters and I did ask him what to do. And he told me, If the situation -- or he did ask me if the situation was threatening or not. And at that moment, it was not threatening at all so we had to stay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you stayed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: At that moment, or after that, I think a couple of minutes, a -- two civilian vehicles arrived with people in military clothes. And I was just about to call my boss again, but I -- they pulled the microphone out of my hand, pulled the keys out of the car, and ordered us to step out of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the soldier that first told you that it was better for you to go phone him -- phone the others, I mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen any communication that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: We were taken on the civilian cars and brought to what I think was a police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have weapons at that moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No, we didn't have weapons at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you pointed at with weapons to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No. The guys were -- they were threatening. They weren't saying anything. They just literally pulled us out of the car, and there were about six of them. So we didn't start anything to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You said that you were led to the police station.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: It looked like a police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the people who were at the police station dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: In both civilian and military clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were many people --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes, it was busy at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: We had to wait in a room or in a hallway for a while. I cannot remember how long. Then we were taken into an office and they asked us a couple of questions, what we were doing at that location and why did we follow the buses. And to me it looked like they were not -- they didn't know really what to do with us. So it took maybe two or three hours that we were at that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two or three hours. And when were you eventually released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: After we were asked the questions, they led us out again. And there was a lot of talking going on in Serbo-Croatian. And we ended up being brought back by two people in civilian, in a very small car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why -- why did you not come back with your vehicle, with your own vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: We weren't allowed to take our own vehicle and all the equipment we had with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of equipment did you have with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: At that moment it was just the military clothing, besides your trousers, shoes, tee shirt, and that was -- the equipment which was on the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how did you get back to the compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: We were brought back in a civilian car, like a little sastava with two men dressed in civilian, and they dropped us off at the gate of the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did they provide you a vehicle to come back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: They drove it. They were on their way to Srebrenica they told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after this event, do you know what happened to the men who were in the buses you attempted to escort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No. At the time we were there, they stayed on the buses and I haven't seen anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: At the time we were at that location until we -- the time the bus stopped until we were taken out of our cars and led to the police station, nothing happened to the men in the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what was the time when -- what was the particular hour, the day, the afternoon, that this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: I have to estimate that, but I think it was around noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around noon. Okay. You are back in the compound and what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes. First we were led out of the car. And in front of the compound it was a little bit more organised, leading people to the buses. And we wanted to enter the compound, but we were not allowed to by the commander who was organising the whole transport.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Sure, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that one commander didn't allow you to enter the compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes. He put us in front of the compound and we had two guards, and they pointed with AK47s at us at that moment. And he ordered them to keep us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: That was around 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the rank of that commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but what I remember it was the same person that normally was at the entrance post of the enclave when we entered or went there for negotiation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what was the name of that major -- I'm sorry, of that commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes. I know that it was Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Because I -- he was always at the entrance point of the enclave when there was an appointment there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Finally what happened? Were you able to come -- to enter the compound or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes. After about an hour they let us go and we went back on the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: We just got another car and hooked up with the convoy again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many buses did this convoy consist of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: There were about -- they were getting a lot smaller because most of it was already out of the enclave. So it was, as far as I remember, only four or five buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened with this second --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: First of all, we were waiting in front of the compound for the next convoy to leave. And we saw a brand new Mercedes all-terrain vehicle passing in front of us with very well-dressed military people in it, and they were looking at our car. And as soon as the buses left, we went after them. And after about 500 metres, the grey Mercedes vehicle was standing on the road with its hood open, and one guy was waving that their car broke down. And as soon as we -- we had to stop because he was blocking the road. We got, again, pulled out of our vehicles. This time I had a gun on my head, and I was pulled out of my vehicle and everything was taken off again. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with that -- with this second convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that convoy was composed of vehicles loaded with men or women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: I cannot clearly remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened with your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: The guys that pulled us out of the vehicle left with the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your vehicle the only one that was stolen that day, apart from the other one and that you had that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No. I think we were losing vehicles with a lot of convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So we can get the gentleman hopefully out of here. Cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. You mentioned Major Nikolic. Now, from listening to your narration, it was my understanding that we're speaking about the 13th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that would have been the second day as opposed to the first day when the buses started leaving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes. The first day was only in the evening, end of the afternoon. So it was the second day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the first day was the 12th, then the second day would have been the 13th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: That would be correct if that's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's your understanding that it was between -- it was around 3.00 to 4.00 in the afternoon when you got back to the compound, and that's when Nikolic decided to -- was acting up the way he did, the way you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you called him a "commander." You don't know, in fact, that he was in command, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No, but I based that on the fact that he was organising the situation there. And according to the first situation, the first convoys, it was organised at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you speak Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know what he was saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know to whom he was -- to who he was speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: He was talking to the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Soldiers --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Or actually, shouting at the two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was he -- during that period on the 12th and the 13th, there were Colonels, Lieutenant Colonels, from the various units, including the corps. Were you aware -- was it your understanding that he was commanding them as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have no questions for this witness but I do have an objection that I need to launch at this point, if the Court will allow me. We have no questions, but based on the proofing notes and the documents that the Prosecution has provided us today, which are ERN numbers -- well, the ERN number 03454898, I want to launch an objection because the circumstances and the methods used by the Prosecutor to interview their witnesses are clearly highly prejudicial and affect the rights of Mr. Jokic to be presumed innocent and to -- under Article 20 and 21, when the witnesses that they're interviewing go by what's equivalent to a mugshot and articles and photographs of the accused on the wall in the areas where they're being interviewed, I think it's highly prejudicial, I think it's improper interview techniques and they should be remedied. If they're going to interview a witness before he testifies they should remove these documents from the wall or make sure that there's no highly suggestive photographs such as mugshots of the accused. I think it's improper and something should be done about it before the next witness is interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we need some explanations from the side of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As the -- I believe the proofing notes show, this witness, like many witnesses, was brought in to an office just to go over things. And on the office wall, pictures have been provided to the Defence. There happened to be a picture of a few of the accused, and this witness recognised one of them. I don't see any problem in that. I don't see any prejudicial effect of it. There hasn't been anything brought out prejudicial to this witness. I don't, frankly, understand the allegation. There's nothing -- nobody's been prejudiced by this in any way. I don't understand what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, I think we received a bunch of the documents with an article, the photos attached to that. And during the direct examination, Mr. Viada did not ask any questions concerning of this document. If you are not going to use this document, why provide us with those documents? I think this action alone could be regarded as prejudicial against the other side. So that's why we need an explanation on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I -- Your Honour, I think the explanation is simple. I can let Mr. Viada do it. I think he just forgot. But I think he can ask, because we -- the reason that these photographs were provided to the Defence was so that it would be completely clear how this witness who spoke of a person in his interviews that he didn't know what the name was, and we did not show him any line-up or anything. It was -- but when he walked through the office, he saw the picture of one of them, of Mr. Nikolic, and said, Yeah, that's the man. Now, that -- we meant to bring that out in direct testimony, and I think just because of the late date and things, it was overlooked. But we can ask Mr. Viada about that. And I know he meant to, that's why these exhibits were here. He wanted to be completely open about how this happened and what it was all about. And I think, like I think all of us have done, sometimes we look down and we realise there's exhibits we've forgotten. But Mr. Viada can speak to that himself, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And before that, I should tend to Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For clarification of the record, the witness did not identify one of the accused in this courtroom. He identified someone who is no longer an accused in this trial. And what I'm trying to prevent is that this does not happen again and interfere and prejudice the testimony of another OTP witness before he's allowed to testify in this courtroom. But the witness -- the articles -- one of the accused was not identified, but someone else was. And I think this is highly prejudicial for them to use these interviewing tactics with these photographs and these mugshots and these articles pasted on their wall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Viada, if you want to ask some questions about those photos, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour. Further examination by Mr. Viada:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, last day in my office you recognised a person, identified an officer, in our office. Can you tell us how this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Well, first of all I was interviewed in the first interview which was I think one and a half, two months ago. And we -- I talked about a person which I couldn't remember the name of. And the second interview, which was on the date we were talking about, the -- I was fighting with the same name, but I couldn't remember the name. And I was being asked if I would recognise him from a picture. And I said that I -- yes, I think so. Because I have seen the man several times at the OP. And right when I walked into that office, I saw a picture on the wall, which I clearly identified him on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did this happen? Were you led to those clippings or were we on a break in our proofing session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: No, we were on a break. I was just looking on the walls, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I would like, with the help of Mr. Usher, to show you an exhibit that has been marked 682. Is that the press clipping?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That you identified the other day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: I have no further questions about this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage -- yes, Mr. Viada.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Yes. Perhaps it should be useful to show also the Exhibit 683, the -- we need the perspective of the room in which the proofing session took place. And tell the witness -- I would like to ask the witness if this is the shape of the wall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the moment you recognised the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-207.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like to, also with the help of Mr. Usher, to show all the rest of these papers --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to him showing all these photographs again. They were not shown to him in the proper environment. Now he's on a fishing expedition. Our objection is that this is improper interviewing techniques and highly suggestive to have these articles in the area where the witness can see them. And now he's going to show them all of them. If he's going to do that, I have one question: If he's going to show him all of the documents which I think is highly improper. If he wants to show the situation in front of the copying machine, that's one thing. If he wants him to identify the one person that he identified, that's another thing. But he did not identify anybody else on the wall. This is just for future interviewing techniques, that it's improper and should not happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I quite understand your objection. Well, if there's objections from the Defence and the witness did not recognise any other persons than the person on the photo you just showed to this witness, I don't think it's necessary to continue this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: I agree with you, Your Honour, but I would like to explain that the circumstances in which these clippings were recognised by the witness was absolutely accidental. These clippings were in our office for a long, long time, and no one could pay attention at this particular moment about these circumstances. Even the witness on the break took the direction to the clippings instead of going out, which is perfectly normal, but these are things that happen. Of course this witness wasn't brought here, hasn't been brought here in order to recognise anybody. The thing is, when he said, Okay, this is the person I met in Potocari that day, we thought in order to be honest with the Defence to say that. Because there was no purpose for this witness to recognise nobody. He had to tell a story. This is something we wanted to explain to the Trial Chamber, because this is -- I can see the relevance of this objection, because -- I mean, there is nothing prejudicial against anything with this particular issue, from my point of view, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- but I believe that the Prosecution should bear the objections from Defence counsel in mind. This kind of practice could not be allowed. In the domestic jurisdictions, the interrogation room or the interview room should be completely clean, without any pictures, photos, which might be suggestive to this case. So I think this should be a warning to you, and in the future to the Defence team that when you are proofing a witness, there should be no pictures, maps, documents, or these kind of things unless, unless, you have some purpose in that proofing session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So I hope you could bear that in mind in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is my responsibility, and I completely understand and take the objection. And it will not happen again. We will not have a witness in the investigative room again. I can promise you that. It was just one of those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I also hope Defence counsel could take this action and the statement from the Prosecution with the bona fide. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour, we do. On behalf of our team here, we do realise it was an accident. And I'm sure that it won't happen again. So we do accept their explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we also accept the -- not apologies, but the explanation of the Prosecution, we just don't want it to happen again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. Is there any redirect on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender into the evidence. Mr. Viada?

utterances.speaker: MR. VIADA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would like to tender the Exhibit P677 and P684.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I can't see the markings, but I assume they're the maps and we have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So these two documents are admitted into the evidence. And P684 under seal. Well thank you very much, Witness, for coming here to give your evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room. We wish you a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, do we have another witness for this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We were conservative because of our problem with time on the next day. So we do not have anymore for this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
